examples.problem_statement: Find the cube root of 76,928,302,277 using single-digit method.

solution.description: Start at the leading group 76: four cubed is 64 is the largest cube below it, so the first root digit a is 4 and the first remainder is 12. Fix the working divisor as three times a squared, that is 48, and keep it for every later column.
Bring down the next digit to make the gross dividend 129. No cross term applies yet, so the adjusted dividend is also 129; dividing by 48 gives the second root digit 2 and remainder 33.
The gross dividend is now 332. Take off the cross term three times a times b squared, which is 48, leaving an adjusted dividend of 284; dividing by 48 gives the third root digit 5 and remainder 44.

With a third root digit in place, the correction for this column is six times a b c plus b cubed, that is 240 plus 8, or 248. Removing it from the gross dividend 448 leaves 200, which yields the fourth root digit 3 and remainder 56.

The four root digits 4, 2, 5, 3 are now fixed, so the remaining columns only have to close out. Here the correction six a b d plus three a c squared plus three b squared c comes to 144 plus 300 plus 60, or 504; subtracting it from the gross dividend 563 leaves 59, recorded with quotient digit 0.

For the next column the correction is six a c d plus three b c squared plus three b squared d, that is 360 plus 150 plus 36, or 546. Taking it from the gross dividend 590 leaves 44, again with quotient digit 0.
This column uses six b c d plus three a d squared plus c cubed: 180 plus 108 plus 125, giving 413. Subtracting from the gross dividend 442 leaves 29, and the quotient digit stays 0.

The last correction is three b d squared plus three c squared d, that is 54 plus 225, or 279. Removing it from the gross dividend 292 leaves 13, so this column too contributes 0 and the schedule ends with the four root digits 4, 2, 5 and 3.

concept.technique_name: Cube root estimation by digit grouping and last-digit clue, checked by bracketing

examples.problem_statement: Find cube root of 9256 using double-digit method and third method.

solution.operation: Group digits in threes from right
solution.description: Mark 9256 off in groups of three from the right, giving 9 and 256, so the root will have two digits.

solution.operation: Find cube root of leftmost group (9)
solution.description: Take the largest whole number whose cube does not exceed the leading group 9. Two cubed is 8 and three cubed is 27, so the tens digit is 2 and the root lies between 20 and 30.

solution.operation: Find units digit using last three digits (256)
solution.description: Read the last-digit clue off the final group 256. Of the single digits only 6 has a cube ending in 6, since 6 cubed is 216, so a perfect cube ending in 6 would have a root ending in 6.
Put the two findings together, the tens digit 2 from the leading group and the units digit 6 from the last-digit clue, for a first estimate of 26.
Check the estimate by cubing it: 26 times 26 is 676, and 676 times 26 is 17576, far above 9256. The last-digit clue has misfired, which is the signal that 9256 is not a perfect cube.
Drop back and try 21 instead: 21 times 21 is 441, and 441 times 21 is 9261, only 5 above the target.
Bracket the answer with the two neighbouring cubes. 21 cubed is 9261, just above 9256, while 20 cubed is 8000, well below, so the cube root sits between 20 and 21.
Since 9256 lies far nearer 9261 than 8000, the cube root rounds to 21. It is an approximation, not an exact root, because 9256 is not a perfect cube.

concept.technique_name: Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem by coordinate geometry

examples.problem_statement: Fifth Proof: Prove Pythagoras' Theorem using Co-ordinate Geometry.

solution.description: Place the right-angled triangle on the coordinate plane with the right angle at the origin, one leg of length a along the x-axis and the other of length b along the y-axis, so the vertices are (0, 0), (a, 0) and (0, b). This turns a statement about lengths into a statement about coordinates.
Apply the distance formula to the two endpoints of the hypotenuse, (a, 0) and (0, b), writing its length as the square root of the squared difference in x plus the squared difference in y.
Square both sides to clear the root and expand the two differences, so the hypotenuse squared becomes a minus 0, squared, plus 0 minus b, squared.
Collect the expanded terms: the hypotenuse squared equals a squared plus b squared, which is exactly the theorem, so the coordinate argument is complete.

concept.technique_name: Two-point form of the equation of a straight line

examples.problem_statement: For finding the Equation of the straight line passing through two points (whose co-ordinates are given. Say, (9, 17) and (7,-2).

solution.description: Label the two given points, taking (9, 17) as the first and (7, -2) as the second. These four numbers are all the method needs.

solution.operation: Apply two-point form of line equation
solution.description: Bring in the two-point form, which states that the slope from the first given point to a general point (x, y) equals the slope between the two given points. That single relation pins the line down.
Substitute the four coordinates. The right-hand side becomes -19 over -2; both differences come out negative, so the slope is positive 19 over 2.
Cross multiply to clear the two denominators, giving 2 times the quantity y minus 17 equal to 19 times the quantity x minus 9.
Distribute on each side: 2 times 17 gives 34 on the left, and 19 times 9 gives 171 on the right.
Move the x term across so the variables sit together on the left and the constants on the right, heading for the Ax plus By equals C shape.
Combine the two constants on the right: -171 plus 34 is -137.

Multiply through by -1 so the leading coefficient is positive, giving 19x minus 2y equals 137. Checking (9, 17) gives 171 minus 34 is 137, and (7, -2) gives 133 plus 4 is 137, so both points lie on the line.
